etymology: From the surname Burgess (a freeman of a borough); borne here by a Westminster divine and author of Spiritual Refining.
biblical_def: Anthony Burgess was a learned Westminster divine and a preacher of unusual weight, who laboured to search the heart and to try the marks of true grace against the counterfeits of hypocrisy and self-deceit. His great work, Spiritual Refining, is a treatise of the nature of true and false grace, wherein he handled the doctrine of assurance, the difference between the regenerate and the merely awakened, and the deceits of a false peace; for he knew that many say Peace, peace when there is no peace, and that the heart is deceitful above all things (Jer 17:9). Against the Antinomians of his day he vindicated the perpetual use of the moral law in the life of the believer — not as a covenant of works whereby to be justified, but as a rule of holiness for the justified, that the law might drive us to Christ and then, being in Christ, direct our walk. The dictionary honours Burgess as a faithful anatomist of the soul, who would not suffer men to rest in a dead profession, but pressed them to prove the reality of the work of God within, that they might make their calling and election sure (2Pe 1:10). He held that saving grace is a new nature wrought by the Spirit, distinct in kind from every glittering imitation, and that the tried Christian, refined as silver, comes forth to praise.
webster_summary: A Westminster divine and searching preacher, author of Spiritual Refining on true and false grace.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of trying true grace from its counterfeits.
corruption_paragraphs: Burgess is preserved in this dictionary because his labour to distinguish true grace from false answers a perennial need of the church, in which many rest upon a fair profession while the root of the matter is not in them. His Spiritual Refining is a searching mercy, forcing the soul off the counterfeit peace of a merely convinced conscience and onto the tried assurance that grows from a new nature wrought by the Spirit.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is discerning self-examination unto assurance — that saving grace differs in kind, not merely degree, from every imitation, and that the moral law abides as the believer’s rule of holiness though never his ground of justification. Where the age flatters men into a shallow peace, Burgess presses the diligence that makes calling and election sure, that the refined soul may come forth as silver from the fire and call upon the name of the LORD.

etymology: From the surname Reynolds (Reginald, ‘counsel-power’); borne by a Westminster divine, later Bishop of Norwich, who penned the General Thanksgiving.
biblical_def: Edward Reynolds was a divine of the Westminster Assembly, a preacher of great eloquence and evangelical warmth, who sat among the framers of the Confession and Catechisms and yet, at the Restoration, conformed and was made Bishop of Norwich. His most enduring gift to the church is the General Thanksgiving, that prayer which blesses God for our creation, preservation, and all the blessings of this life, but above all for His inestimable love in the redemption of the world by our Lord Jesus Christ, for the means of grace, and for the hope of glory. Herein Reynolds gathered the whole compass of mercy into a single confession of praise, that we might show forth His praise not only with our lips but in our lives. He wrote also a rich exposition upon the hundred-and-tenth Psalm and a treatise on the sinfulness of sin, tracing the corruption of our nature to its bitter root. The dictionary honours Reynolds for his labour at the Assembly and for teaching generations to give thanks, holding that in every thing we are to give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning us (1Th 5:18). His conformity we note without concealing it, yet his catechetical labour and his thankful spirit remain a heritage to the whole church, teaching that the redeemed have cause to bless the LORD at all times.

corruption_summary: A faithful teacher of thanksgiving, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of grateful praise for redemption.
corruption_paragraphs: Reynolds is preserved because he taught the church to number its mercies and to bless God chiefly for the redemption purchased in Christ. The General Thanksgiving he composed still gathers creation, preservation, and above all inestimable redeeming love into one confession of praise, schooling the redeemed to give thanks in every thing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is grateful praise as the will of God for His people — that we bless the LORD at all times and forget not His benefits, chief of which is the redemption of the world by our Lord Jesus Christ. His later conformity we note plainly, without pretending it was nothing; yet his catechetical labour at the Assembly and his thankful spirit teach the whole church that the redeemed have endless cause to show forth His praise, in word and deed alike.

etymology: From the surname Greenhill (dweller by a green hill); borne by a Westminster divine famed for his exposition of Ezekiel.
biblical_def: William Greenhill was a divine of the Westminster Assembly, an Independent by conviction and a faithful pastor, whose life-labour was a vast and searching exposition of the prophecy of Ezekiel, opened chapter by chapter with great care and spiritual profit. In that dark book of visions and woes he traced the glory of the LORD departing from a polluted temple and returning again to a temple restored, the watchman set to warn the wicked from his way (Eze 3:17), the valley of dry bones made to live by the breath of the Spirit (Eze 37), and the sure promise of a new heart and a new spirit given to God’s covenant people. Greenhill taught that the God who threatens judgment upon impenitent men also swears He hath no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Eze 33:11). The dictionary honours Greenhill as a diligent expositor who fed the flock upon the whole counsel of God, refusing to pass by the harder prophets, and who pressed upon his hearers the watchman’s solemn charge to warn, and the gospel promise that the LORD Himself will give a heart of flesh in place of the heart of stone.

corruption_summary: A faithful expositor, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of preaching the whole counsel of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Greenhill is preserved because his life was given to opening a difficult prophet whom lesser men neglect, feeding the flock upon the whole counsel of God rather than the easy portions only. His Ezekiel labours the watchman’s solemn charge to warn and the sovereign promise of a new heart, keeping both the terror and the tenderness of God before the reader.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the diligent, unabridged exposition of Scripture — that the pastor must warn the wicked from his way as a watchman answerable for blood, and must proclaim the covenant mercy whereby the LORD takes away the stony heart and gives a heart of flesh. Regeneration is here shown to be God’s own act, dry bones raised by His breath alone, that no man may boast; and this Greenhill preached faithfully, sparing neither the woe nor the wonder of the vision.

etymology: From the surname Hardy (bold, enduring); borne by a London preacher noted for his exposition of the First Epistle of John.
biblical_def: Nathanael Hardy was a preacher of London in the seventeenth century, a man of learning and diligence whose chief monument is a large and warm exposition of the First Epistle of John, wherein he opened that Epistle of love and light with pastoral care. Following the apostle, Hardy pressed the great tests of eternal life — that God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all (1Jo 1:5); that the blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanseth us from all sin; that hereby we know that we are of the truth if we love the brethren; and that the beloved of God should not love the world, neither the things that are in the world. He taught assurance not as presumption but as the fruit of obedience and love, for he that keepeth His commandments dwelleth in Him, and God in him. The dictionary honours Hardy as a faithful expositor who fed the church upon the milk and marrow of an apostolic letter, holding forth the incarnate Word made manifest, the propitiation for our sins, and the perfect love that casteth out fear. He would have his hearers know that they had eternal life, that they might believe on the name of the Son of God, and walk in the light as He is in the light.

corruption_summary: A faithful expositor, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of assurance grounded in obedient love.
corruption_paragraphs: Hardy is preserved because his exposition of First John holds together what men are ever tempted to divide — the free cleansing of the blood of Christ and the necessary fruit of walking in the light. He pressed the apostle’s tests of true faith, that believers might know they have eternal life without either despairing or presuming.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is assurance grounded in obedient love — that God is light, that the blood of Jesus Christ cleanseth from all sin, and that we know we are of the truth when we love the brethren and keep His commandments. Against a cheap profession that never bears fruit, Hardy insists on the marks; against an anxious legalism, he holds forth the perfect love that casteth out fear. He would have the church walk in the light, as He is in the light, and so have fellowship one with another.

etymology: From the surname Spurstowe (of a place-name origin); borne by a Westminster divine and one of the authors of Smectymnuus.
biblical_def: William Spurstowe was a divine of the Westminster Assembly and one of the five authors whose initials formed the tract Smectymnuus, that famous defence of the Presbyterian government of elders against the claims of prelacy; the final letters of the name are his own. A learned and devout pastor, he was among those ejected from his living at the Great Ejection of sixteen hundred and sixty-two, choosing the loss of his place before conformity against conscience. His pen served the flock also in warmer works of devotion, most notably a treatise upon the promises of God, wherein he gathered up the exceeding great and precious promises whereby the saints are made partakers of the divine nature (2Pe 1:4), showing that in Christ all the promises of God are yea, and in Him Amen (2Co 1:20). The dictionary honours Spurstowe for his labour at the Assembly, his defence of the New Testament eldership, and his steadfast nonconformity; but chiefly for teaching the church to live upon the promises, feeding faith not upon feeling but upon the sure word of a God who cannot lie. He stands among the Westminster worthies who gave the church her confession and catechisms, and who counted the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of ease.
webster_summary: A Westminster divine, a Smectymnuus author, ejected in 1662, who wrote on the promises of God.

corruption_summary: A faithful divine, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of living upon the sure promises of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Spurstowe is preserved because he joined a sound defence of the New Testament eldership with a rich devotional labour upon the promises of God. His treatise taught the saints to feed faith upon the sure word rather than upon shifting feeling, for in Christ all the promises are yea and Amen.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is living faith upon the promises of God — the exceeding great and precious promises whereby believers become partakers of the divine nature and escape the corruption that is in the world. His steadfast nonconformity at the Great Ejection shows the same faith at work, choosing the loss of his living before a conformity his conscience could not bear. The Westminster worthies gave the church her confession, and many, Spurstowe among them, sealed their fidelity with the loss of place and ease.

etymology: From the surname Bolton (a place-name, ‘dwelling settlement’); borne by a Westminster divine and author of The True Bounds of Christian Freedom.
biblical_def: Samuel Bolton was a divine of the Westminster Assembly and Master of Christ’s College in Cambridge, whose most abiding work, The True Bounds of Christian Freedom, set the golden mean between the two ditches of legalism and Antinomianism. He taught that the believer is set free from the law as a covenant of works, from its curse and condemning power, from its rigour and its dominion as a way of justification; yet the moral law abides as a rule of holy living, so that grace does not abolish obedience but establishes it. Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, he urged, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage (Gal 5:1); and yet, use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another (Gal 5:13). Bolton showed that Christian freedom is freedom to serve God without slavish fear, freedom of a son and not a hireling, purchased by the blood of Christ who redeemed us from the curse of the law. The dictionary honours Bolton for mapping the true bounds of gospel liberty, holding that we are freed from the law that we might be married to another, even to Him who is raised from the dead, that we should bring forth fruit unto God.

corruption_summary: A faithful teacher of liberty, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the true bounds of Christian freedom.
corruption_paragraphs: Bolton is preserved because he charted the narrow way between two abiding errors: the legalism that would put believers back under the law as a covenant of works, and the Antinomianism that would abolish the law altogether as a rule of life. His True Bounds of Christian Freedom keeps both ditches in view, defining a liberty that is freedom to serve God as sons, not licence to sin.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the true bounds of Christian liberty — that Christ has freed us from the law’s curse and condemnation, yet its precepts abide as the believer’s rule of holiness. Where a corrupt age turns freedom into a pretext for the flesh, Bolton answers that we are called unto liberty only that by love we might serve one another, being dead to the law that we might be married to the risen Christ and bring forth fruit unto God. Whom the Son makes free is free indeed — free to obey.

etymology: From the surname Ball; borne by a Puritan divine whose Treatise of the Covenant of Grace deeply shaped Westminster federal theology.
biblical_def: John Ball was a Puritan divine of great learning and holiness, a maker of catechisms and, above all, the author of A Treatise of the Covenant of Grace, a work that laboured to set forth the covenant which God made with man in Christ, and which fed the federal theology afterward gathered into the Westminster standards. Ball taught that the whole of Scripture is unfolded by the two covenants, the covenant of works made with Adam, which he brake, and the covenant of grace made in Christ the second Adam, ordered in all things and sure (2Sa 23:5), whereby God promises to be a God unto us and to our seed. He held that this covenant is one in substance under law and gospel, administered diversely but ever resting upon the same Mediator and the same free promise, I will be their God, and they shall be my people (Jer 31:33). His catechism trained households in the faith, that fathers might teach their children the things of God. The dictionary honours Ball as a father of covenant theology, whose careful labour taught the church to read her Bible by the covenants, and to rest her whole hope upon the grace that God swore to His people in His Son, an everlasting covenant that shall not be removed.

He held forth one covenant of grace, one Mediator, and one free promise beneath the diverse administrations of law and gospel.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the covenant of grace as the key to Scripture — that God, having made a covenant of works with Adam which he brake, established in Christ the second Adam an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and sure, wherein He is a God to His people and to their seed. His catechism served the same end, arming fathers to teach their children the faith; and this catechetical, covenantal labour remains a heritage to the church, that she might rest her whole salvation upon the grace God swore in His Son.

etymology: From the given name Immanuel (Hebrew, ‘God with us’) and the surname Bourne (dweller by a stream); borne by a long-lived Puritan minister of Derbyshire.
biblical_def: Immanuel Bourne was a Puritan minister of Derbyshire, a preacher of remarkable length of days, whose ministry spanned the reigns of many princes and the great upheavals of his age, labouring on in the country parish through changing times with a steadfast fidelity. His very name, Immanuel, is the name of the promised Child, God with us (Isa 7:14; Mat 1:23), a standing sermon that the whole hope of the church rests upon the incarnate Lord who tabernacled among us. Bourne wrote in defence of gospel truth and against the errors that troubled his day, and gave himself to the long, unglamorous work of preaching and catechizing a flock over the course of a very long pilgrimage. The dictionary honours Bourne for his perseverance in the ministry, an example of the servant found faithful over many years and not merely in a season, who having put his hand to the plough looked not back (Luk 9:62). His length of days in the work bears witness that the Lord who is Immanuel keeps His labourers, and that the crown is promised not to the swift beginning but to the faithful end — be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life (Rev 2:10). A long life spent in the vineyard is itself a testimony to God with us.

corruption_paragraphs: Bourne is preserved because his long life in a country ministry embodies the perseverance the age most despises — the patient, unglamorous work of preaching and catechizing one flock through decades of change and turmoil. His very name, Immanuel, keeps before us the ground of all such fidelity, God with us in Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is perseverance in the ministry — that the servant is required to be found faithful not for a season only but unto the end, having put his hand to the plough and not looking back. His name preaches the incarnate Lord, God with us, who keeps His labourers to the last; and the promise stands over every faithful pilgrim, be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. A long life spent in the vineyard is a sermon in itself.

etymology: From the given name Nathaniel (Hebrew, ‘gift of God’) and the surname Vincent (Latin, ‘conquering’); borne by an ejected Puritan, brother of Thomas Vincent.
biblical_def: Nathaniel Vincent was a Puritan minister and one of the two thousand ejected at the Great Ejection of sixteen hundred and sixty-two, the younger brother of Thomas Vincent, and a preacher who suffered imprisonment more than once for the offence of preaching Christ outside the bounds of conformity. A man of fervent spirit, he pressed upon sinners the necessity of the new birth and upon saints the duty of a heavenly walk, and gave himself to the persecuted meetings of the nonconformists in perilous times, when to gather for worship was to hazard fine, prison, and worse. His pen served the same cause, urging the fear of God, the making sure of an interest in Christ, and the beauty of holiness. The dictionary honours Nathaniel Vincent as a suffering witness of the ejected ministry, who counted the reproach of Christ greater riches than the ease that conformity would have bought, and who esteemed the recompence of the reward (Heb 11:26). He knew that all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution (2Ti 3:12), and he embraced that word, blessed among those persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. In him the church sees the cost, and the crown, of a good confession.

corruption_summary: A suffering witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the cost and crown of a good confession.
corruption_paragraphs: Nathaniel Vincent is preserved because his imprisonments and his labour among the outlawed nonconformist meetings show the true cost of a good confession. When conformity would have bought him ease, he chose the reproach of Christ and the recompence of the reward, obeying God rather than men.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the cost and crown of faithfulness — that all who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution, and that the persecuted for righteousness’ sake are blessed, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. His willingness to preach the new birth at the hazard of fine and prison rebukes every generation that treats obedience as negotiable when it grows costly. The church remembers Nathaniel Vincent, with his brother Thomas, as a witness that we ought to obey God rather than men, and that the reproach of Christ is greater riches than the treasures of ease.

etymology: From the given name Thomas (Aramaic, ‘twin’) and the surname Vincent (Latin, ‘conquering’); borne by the ejected Puritan author of The Shorter Catechism Explained.
biblical_def: Thomas Vincent was an ejected Puritan minister of London, brother of Nathaniel, best known for his catechetical labour An Explicatory Catechism, or an Explanation of the Assembly’s Shorter Catechism, wherein he opened the questions and answers of that little book for households and children, that the young might be grounded in the first principles of the oracles of God. When the dreadful plague fell upon London in sixteen hundred and sixty-five, and many conforming ministers had fled the stricken city, Vincent, though himself silenced and ejected, went back into the deserted pulpits to preach to the dying, and afterward set down his warnings in God’s Terrible Voice in the City, calling the survivors to repentance beneath the twin scourges of plague and fire. He knew that except men repent, they shall all likewise perish (Luk 13:3), and that it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb 10:31). The dictionary honours Vincent as a faithful catechist and a fearless preacher of judgment and mercy, who fed the lambs with plain doctrine and warned the careless with the voice of God in the storm, so that men might flee to Christ, the only refuge from the wrath to come.

corruption_summary: A faithful catechist and preacher of judgment, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers plain instruction and the call to repent.
corruption_paragraphs: Vincent is preserved because he joined two labours the church ever needs: the patient catechizing of households in plain doctrine, and the fearless preaching of repentance under judgment. His explanation of the Shorter Catechism grounded the young in the faith, while his return to plague-stricken London to preach to the dying showed a shepherd who would not flee his flock.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is catechesis joined to the solemn call to repent — that we teach the truths of God diligently to our children as newborn babes desiring the sincere milk of the word, and that we warn the careless, for except they repent they shall all likewise perish. His God’s Terrible Voice in the City reads the plague and fire as God’s summons to flee to Christ from the wrath to come, holding forth both the terror of falling into the hands of the living God and the mercy set before the penitent. His courage in the stricken city rebukes every hireling who forsakes the sheep.
